name: Mosel

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, warm summer

climate: Seasons this cool ripen Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewürztraminer fully without cooking off their freshness.
Riesling and Müller-Thurgau sit in their sweet spot, so the wines can show the style they are known for.

soil.rock: Shale and mudstone are fine-grained rocks that hold heat well and are moderately fertile.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its pH is close to neutral, so vines take up the nutrients they need easily.

land: The high ground runs about 3°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Much of it is steep. Cold air and rain run off, so frost and waterlogging are rare and soils stay thin, keeping yields low. Steep rows are slow and costly to work, often by hand.

winkler: Only very early grapes ripen well, mostly hybrids and a few vinifera.

sheet.place: The Mosel is a cool German river valley with steep slate slopes facing south. Riesling ripens slowly here. The wines come out light in alcohol, high in acid and balanced by a little sugar.
sheet.rules: German wine is graded by how ripe the grapes were, not how sweet the wine is. On the Mosel, Riesling needs at least 73 Oechsle for Kabinett, 80 for Spätlese and 88 for Auslese. Beerenauslese and Eiswein start at 110, Trockenbeerenauslese at 150.

claims.claim: The region is named after the Mosel river. It was called Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 1 August 2007, then shortened to Mosel.

The PDO covers vines along the Mosel and its tributaries Saar and Ruwer. The river runs from Perl on the Luxembourg border to Koblenz. The spec splits it into Obermosel, Trierer Talweitung, Mittelmosel (Schweich to Moselkern) and the lower valley.

Wine law divides the region into Bereiche (districts). Wikipedia lists Burg Cochem, Bernkastel, Ruwertal, Saar, Obermosel and Moseltor. Bernkastel is the centre of the Mittelmosel. Saar and Ruwer are the two side valleys.
Graach (Himmelreich), Wehlen (Klosterberg, Sonnenuhr) and Zeltingen (Sonnenuhr) are neighbouring wine villages on the Mittelmosel, in the Bernkastel district.

Vines on the Mosel, Saar and Ruwer grow between about 65 and 375 m above sea level, averaging about 180 m. About half the vineyards face south-east, south or south-west. The average aspect is 195 degrees, which is south-south-west.

Devonian rock dominates the region. From Mittelmosel downstream the river cuts a narrow valley into the Rhenish Slate Mountains. The Devonian rocks are mostly quartzitic sandstone, quartzite and clay slate. Limestone (Muschelkalk, Keuper) appears only on the Obermosel.
Slate soils warm quickly and drain well, and many top sites have little topsoil, only broken slate. Slate type varies by site and shapes the wine's mineral character.

Slate is described by colour: blue slate on the Mosel proper, grey slate on the Saar, and some red slate with more clay. This colour split comes from wine-guide summaries and the VDP register uses 'blue and grey' for Himmelreich.

The steep slopes give the vines the most direct sunlight in the region. Average direct sun in the growing season is 652,000 Wh/m2, highest on steep and very steep sites. The river also reflects light onto the vines.

The steepest vineyard in the world is thought to be Bremmer Calmont on the lower Mosel, at about 65 degrees. The three sheet vineyards are less extreme. VDP slopes are 45 to 75 percent (Himmelreich) and 65 to 75 percent (Zeltinger Sonnenuhr).
The climate is cool. Average annual temperature is 9.7 C and the growing-season average is 14.1 C. Rainfall averages 760 mm a year, 60 percent of it in the growing season.

The sheltered river valley and the water moderate the climate, so it is mild for its latitude. Autumn nights bring fog as cold air from Hunsrück and Eifel meets warmer air over the river. The fog burns off by midday. Slow ripening and big day-night swings give fine fruit and a sharp, precise acidity.

Riesling is the main grape. It covered 59.7 percent of the region's vines in 2008 (5,390 ha), well ahead of Müller-Thurgau at 14 percent. Total area then was about 9,034 ha, the fifth largest of Germany's 13 regions.

Mosel Riesling is known for moderate alcohol, marked acidity and a balance of sweetness and acid. The spec says grapes reach only moderate sugar even at full ripeness, giving delicate wines with moderate alcohol. It describes Kabinett as having low to moderate alcohol and tense acid-sweet balance, and Spätlese and Auslese as usually made with some residual sugar. Typical aromas are pome fruit, stone fruit and citrus.
The steep slate slopes favour botrytis in ripe, humid autumns, which allows selection of Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.

Six Prädikat levels, set by must weight (ripeness at harvest, not final sweetness). Minimum for Mosel Riesling: Kabinett 73 Oechsle (9.5% vol potential), Spätlese 80 (10.6%), Auslese 88 (11.9%), Beerenauslese 110 (15.3%), Eiswein 110 (15.3%), Trockenbeerenauslese 150 (21.5%).

Eiswein grapes must be naturally frozen at harvest and pressing. Beerenauslese uses overripe, dried or botrytised berries. Trockenbeerenauslese uses more selection and shrivelled berries, giving the highest sweetness.
The Mosel Riesling minimums are higher than the older commonly quoted German figures of Kabinett 67-70, Spätlese 76 and Auslese 83. The Mosel PDO spec sets 73, 80 and 88 for Riesling.

Graacher Himmelreich is in the village of Graach, a VDP.GROSSE LAGE planted to Riesling. It faces south-west to south, lies at 110 to 325 m, and has a slope of 45 to 75 percent. Soil is blue and grey slate. Graded area is listed as 163.09 acres, about 66 ha.

Zeltinger Sonnenuhr is in Zeltingen. It is a VDP.GROSSE LAGE planted to Riesling, facing south-south-west to south, at 100 to 250 m, with a slope of 65 to 75 percent. Soil is stony, weathered grey Devonian slate. Graded area is 51.25 acres, about 21 ha.
Zeltinger Sonnenuhr is named for a large sundial in the vines, built in 1620 by an abbot of Himmerod Monastery. It is billed as the largest sundial in a German vineyard.

Do not mix up the two Sonnenuhr sites. Wehlener Sonnenuhr is in Wehlen, graded at 113.67 acres (about 46 ha), grey-blue Devonian slate, 110 to 320 m. Zeltinger Sonnenuhr is a separate, smaller site two villages away.

Wehlener Klosterberg is a slope in Wehlen, beside Markus Molitor's family house, Haus Klosterberg, which sits at the top. An importer describes it as a large, classically oriented slope with iron-rich Devonian slate. No official size, slope or exact aspect was found.
Molitor's own Wehlener Klosterberg holding was given as 6.4 ha in a 2001 note, his Zeltinger Sonnenuhr holding as 5.1 ha. These are the estate's parcels, not the whole Einzellage.

gaps: No official size, aspect, slope or soil for Wehlener Klosterberg. The VDP register and search results did not cover it.
No official size or soil for the legal Einzellagen (as opposed to VDP graded areas) for any of the three. The state Weinbergsrolle was not read.
Origin of the name Himmelreich (Graach) not found. Origin of Klosterberg not confirmed beyond the monastery-slope sense of the word.
Name origin of 'Mosel' (Latin Mosella) not sourced.
Bereich membership of Graach, Wehlen and Zeltingen, and the Bernkasteler Ring, not confirmed by a fetched source.
Current Riesling share and vineyard area are not found; Wikipedia gives 2008.
Several sources (winewithseth, Jancis Robinson, wein.plus, Meininger) were blocked or rate-limited when fetched.
